newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan PM pledges to speed market reforms in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Jordan PM pledges to speed market reforms in 1997.

text.p: Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul Karim al-Kabariti pledged on Monday to help speed the passing of a new securities law in 1997 to reform the market.

The official Amman Financial Market 60-share index rose 1.20 percent to 153.46 points in high turnover of 1,733,989 dinars ($2.4 million) dominated by stepped up portfolio buying in year-end window dressing that helped cap a disappointing year, dealers said.

Kabariti said during a visit to the bourse on Monday, the year's last day of 1996 trade, that the government wanted a speedy passage of a new securities law that will radically reform its bourse to help it compete regionally.

Kabariti was quoted by the state news agency Petra as saying the government may resort to passing the bill by other constitutional means if time does not allow the current parliamentary session which ends in April to pass it.
The new securities law, part of Jordan's wider IMF backed reforms, sets up a government watchdog the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) to oversee a restructured private-sector run market.

Kabariti also urged investors and brokers to lobby parliamentarians on the importance of the swift passage of the law, along with other legislation including an overhauled companies law, to help activate the market.
A total of 248,498,666 dinars of stock changed hands this year, a 40 percent drop from the previous year with the market hit by a combination of political uncertainty and a high interest rate policy.
Investors say the law will help raise the market's profile to foreign investors who have shied from investing large amounts despite eased rules on ownership of stock.
Kabariti made no mention of monetary policy or easing in high interest rates policy which many brokers blame as a key factor behind diverting funds to higher yield bank deposits.

Investors said the market's turnover on Monday was dominated by artificially bolstered portfolio buying to prop up closing prices to reduce loss provisions for 1996 stock price falls that averaged around 12 percent.
Brokers said end-of-year window dressing accounted for most of the trade in such stock as Jordan Gulf Bank, International Tobacco and Jordan Cement Factories and Middle East Investment Bank.

"It's window dressing regarding the closing prices for year-end to minimise the provisions that should be taken by institutions and provident funds investing in the Amman Financial Market (AFM)," said Nasser al-Amad, heading United Financial Investments brokerage firm.
They also said the last month of the year's performance of the cash squeezed market pointed towards a weak start for 1997 and capped an overall disappointing year.

Investors hopes were dashed when a brief rebound this month in the wake of Iraq's oil-for-food deal on raised hopes of business opportunities that would breathe new life into the Amman bourse lost steam.
